evals.prompt: I need to create a Facebook ad image for Folqs colostrum. We're targeting gut health problem-aware women 35-55 who've tried probiotics before and nothing worked. What should the ad look like?
evals.expected_output: A structured Design Brief with: visual pattern selected from the library, layout with visual hierarchy, color palette with psychological rationale, face/person decision with emotional state, product placement, CTA button spec, reference image filenames, and a complete Gemini prompt ready to execute.

assertions.text: Response includes a labeled Design Brief with distinct sections (Layout, Color, Face/Person, Product Placement, CTA)
assertions.description: Checks for structured output format — not just prose suggestions

assertions.text: Response explicitly assigns an awareness level (L1-L5) and ties at least one design decision to it
assertions.description: Framework vocabulary must appear — proves the skill is guiding the response

assertions.text: Each major design decision (color, layout, face) includes a psychological rationale — not just what, but why
assertions.description: Design decisions must be traceable to a reason, not arbitrary

assertions.text: Response includes a Gemini-executable prompt or states it is Gemini-ready
assertions.description: Production deliverable — the output must be actionable, not just advisory

evals.prompt: We have copy for a new ad. Awareness level L2, shame hook, social proof as the dominant bias. It's for a men's hair loss supplement targeting guys 30-50 who are just starting to notice thinning. What visual pattern should I use and why?
evals.expected_output: Pattern recommendation mapped to L2 awareness + shame hook + social proof bias. Should include: specific pattern name, design rationale tied to the copy signal, color recommendation, face/before-after decision, and why this pattern beats alternatives.

assertions.text: Response maps L2 awareness level to a specific visual approach (problem-state visualization, not product hero)
assertions.description: Core framework mapping — L2 should never result in a product-forward ad

assertions.text: Response addresses how the shame hook translates to visual choices (face emotional state, minimal copy, problem-state imagery)
assertions.description: Shame hook must influence the design direction explicitly

assertions.text: Response explains how social proof bias appears visually (faces + numbers, before/after, NOT clinical/logo-based)
assertions.description: Bias-to-visual mapping must be specific and correct

assertions.text: Response explains why at least one alternative pattern FAILS for this combination
assertions.description: Anti-pattern reasoning demonstrates deep framework understanding vs. generic advice

evals.prompt: Analyze this — ColonBroom runs a dark mode premium ad (dark navy background, clean product shot, minimal text). It's been running 61+ days. What design psychology makes this work and when should we use this approach?
evals.expected_output: Design psychology analysis citing specific principles, correct awareness level fit (L4-L5), clear 'when NOT to use' with specific scenarios (TOF cold, L2 problem-aware, sub-$20 price points).

assertions.text: Response cites at least 2 named psychological principles (e.g., pattern interrupt, visual cortex processing, premium positioning, fluency heuristic, Z-pattern)
assertions.description: Analysis must be grounded in specific principles, not vague impressions

assertions.text: Response identifies this as appropriate for L4-L5 audience awareness — NOT for cold TOF traffic
assertions.description: Correct Titan framework placement — this is a closing/retargeting pattern

assertions.text: Response includes a 'when NOT to use' section with specific contra-indicators
assertions.description: Directional guidance is only useful if it also tells you when to avoid it
